items.question: How do you view the idea that Google Duplex's 2018 demonstration represented artificial general intelligence?
items.object: Google Duplex and its reception as artificial general intelligence
items.answer: I've been on the Google Duplex team. What we've done in the Duplex project was pretty different from visual stuff because it was mostly getting stuff done over the phone. The Duplex project was, if people remember from Google I/O 2018, people thought, "Okay, wow, we have AGI." It was one of the, "Is it AGI?" moments, but I think probably not.
quotes: Then I joined Google and I've been on the Google Duplex team. What we've done in the Duplex project was pretty different from visual stuff because it was mostly getting stuff done over the phone.
The Duplex project was, if people remember from Google I/O 2018, people thought, "Okay, wow, we have AGI." It was one of the, "Is it AGI?" moments, but I don't think probably not.

rubrics.text: The response judges that Google Duplex’s 2018 demonstration probably did not represent artificial general intelligence.

items.question: How do you assess what Google Duplex was able to accomplish?
items.object: Google Duplex
items.answer: When we started Duplex, the goal was actually a question of, can we build already today a bot that talks over the phone with people without them feeling this is actually a machine, and hitting this kind of maybe over-the-phone Turing test, if you want. What we found is that although having a completely general conversation over the phone was not achievable until very recently with LLMs, already then—and that was the era of RNNs, LSTMs, and definitely not transformers—we were able to develop something that, at least for this particular task, accomplished a lot of tasks. That was my first touch with machine learning, and it was very interesting because it was also very research-oriented, but also had a deployment in the real world. We ended up scaling that to call hundreds of millions of calls over, overall, 15 countries.

items.object: The revolution in image diffusion models
items.answer: I also, of course, followed things that happened on the LLM side, from GPT and internally at Google. We had Mina and LaMDA and other models very early on. Then we kind of integrated this technology into Google Duplex, but at some point I just felt that maybe my visual roots came into play again, and the revolution in image diffusion models was really appealing to me. I just felt like this is a huge opportunity. It's really something that's hitting some kind of point of maturity.

items.question: What were you excited to explore with your neural-network game engine side project?
items.object: Real-time game simulation entirely by a neural network
items.answer: I've been working on video models. One incarnation of that was a game engine, which was a bit of a side project. We were very excited, me and a few friends. items.question: How do you think about what makes a model a world model?
items.object: World models and their relationship to visual simulation
items.answer:
I'm coming more from simulation. I think about more the visual. What we call world models today are very visual-specific, which I think is one of the limitations of current world models. But if we go back to the World Models paper Jack mentioned, again, the definition was pretty clear, and I think it's a good definition to start from and anchor to because the term is definitely used in many ways. But I think there is also a bit of an intuition to it, which of course can be formalized. From my perspective, when I started seeing video models, but also image models, when you write text, provide a text prompt, and then you see something, it feels like there is a world behind those pixels. For things to really look like a realistic image or video, the model probably has to have some internal representation of what's going on, how the world behaves, our physics to some extent. That's the intuition behind the world model in layman's terms: the model probably has some understanding of the world, and it's visual.

But the world model doesn't have to be visual. It doesn't have to be something that generates pixels. In some of the literature, the world model can be in some latent space. It should be something we can use to make decisions and predict what's going to happen next, and maybe perform planning in RL and learn how to operate in a more optimal way in an environment. Going back to the visual domain, I think what happened is the visual domain really worked well because diffusion models happened to work really well for images, videos, and audio as well. This intersection between those fields became very obvious. I think that's where we are right now: we have models capable of generating very realistic environments, and we're trying to push along this thing.

items.question: How did you think about taking Genie 3 to the next level?
items.object: Genie 3’s research ambition
items.answer:
Basically, in Genie 3, we really tried to push it to the limit across all of the dimensions. If we see the progression Jack just talked about, we have models that are more capable in terms of the quality of their generation. Genie 1 and Genie 2 are able to generate more and more worlds that are more consistent, but still to a limit. We wanted to push how long this trajectory can remain consistent. That was one of the dimensions we wanted to improve. And of course, the resolution. If you look at the resolution, the duration of the interaction, how fast the next frame can be generated, if you multiply all of those dimensions, you get quite a 100x improvement in raw compute. It was very clear this was not something obvious that was going to work, so there was some risk to this project, but we also felt this is the time to go for it.

After we launched Veo 2, it was very well received. We felt like the quality really improved, but it was definitely not real-time or interactive. Then Genie 2 came out and also pushed the envelope in a different direction. We said, "Okay, let's try and combine those vectors of improvement and go to the next level." That's pretty much what Genie 3 is about, trying to bring the best of all worlds, pun intended, maybe.

items.question: How do you understand the consistency challenge shared by video generators like Veo and interactive world models like Genie?
items.object: Consistency in video generation and interactive world models
items.answer: We generate output that's eventually pixels, take text as input, and want to generate something that feels consistent. Even if it's a video of eight seconds, like Veo generates, you still want to feel that it's consistent. If the camera moves around, things should look consistent. You need to get a feel that this was taken maybe in the real world. The same goes once it's interactive. We want to generate the next frame based on the user's input, but consistency is really important. There were some early models that were able to generate the next frame. Game Engine in a way was that. It didn't have very long context, and the reason it worked is because it learned specific properties of the game Doom. It kind of remembered how the level looks, so it wasn't really generating it as we would want.

items.question: Why do you see text as the right starting point for generating an interactive world in Genie 3?
items.object: Text as the starting point for generating interactive worlds
items.answer: Being able to generate things from text is the core capability that you see from image models to video models. I think that was the main innovation breakthrough for all of this line of research: text became how you could start. Text is such a compressed representation, and such a strong way to learn concepts. It was obvious that we start from text this time. We want to describe the world, then drop you into it, and let the user or agent go around and explore it. Those are the similarities of the projects.

items.question: How did your goal of real-time interactivity shape the architecture of Genie 3?
items.object: Real-time interactivity as the guiding principle for Genie 3's architecture
items.answer:
One of the key aspects of the model is it is basically autoregressive, which in this context means that the next frame is generated based on the long sequence, potentially long sequence, of everything that happened before. The model has to look at what happened before the particular frame, reason over this past, and decide which information is relevant to the next frame. The key is that it has to happen very quickly. That has to happen multiple times per second because we can never know what the next actions from the user are going to be. I think this is what makes it real-time interactive, not just real-time.

This term is really what led our design of the system and architecture: interactivity while being real-time. Everything boils down to that kind of design decision. To get to this very low latency and be able to look back into what happened before, that's what made us look into how we can leverage and pick the right architecture and scale that enables both a very high-quality model and leveraging the best-in-class hardware we have to build something that works. It's not just a theoretical system or something that might be a paper, but actually something that we hope eventually will be able to share with more people in the future.

items.question: How do you approach achieving consistency in the Genie 3 world model without an explicit representation of the world?
items.object: Consistency in the Genie 3 world model
items.answer: That was definitely our goal and we definitely designed it in a way to achieve this goal. When we listed what we wanted in the spec of the model, definitely a memory of about one minute was in it. That was our goal. But the key thing is that there's no explicit representation of the world. There are a lot of approaches where you can implement, for example, a 3D engine that has a very explicit mesh, and then this gets rendered and you can go anywhere you want. It has a lot of limitations but also amazing applications. In the machine learning world, you have NeRFs and Gaussian splats, and that derives some representation of the geometry of the world. Based on that you can walk around and everything gets rendered. These are all explicit representations, and we didn't want to do that. While they do have a lot of applications, they're also limited. It's much harder to have dynamic environments, and we wanted the model to learn that on its own. We didn't think we should build anything into the system to achieve it. I think we're good students of the Bitter Lesson, and we believe that, at least I believe, many of those things can be learned from data alone if you design the system in a way that's set up to learn those capabilities.

items.question: Why do you see Genie's promptable world events as a deep capability?
items.object: Genie's promptable world events
items.answer: We do have these promptable world events that allow you to just make a change in the world and inject some new information. That allows control of the world beyond just the prompt provided in the beginning. This is more of a temporarily local thing. It's quite a deep capability, I think, because it's not obvious that the prompt always makes sense. For example, you say, "Okay, a door opens," and you're in the middle of the desert. What door should open? The model is like, "I don't know." We see that sometimes it can make weird stuff because the model is trying to, but when it makes sense, we often see that it does work. We have some very nice samples, like the dragon that appears out of the sky and lands in the middle of the tunnel. There are definitely some cases where it works really well and it's a very powerful capability.

items.question: How do you think promptable world events should fit into the world generated by Genie 3?
items.object: Promptable world events in Genie 3
items.answer: We think this is an event. If you think about walking around the world, things happen around us. They're not necessarily done by us; they're not agent-centric. It's not just based on a single frame. It can be that you want to see something in the world, and then you look to the left and see, for example, a person. We have examples where you ski down the slopes, and then you look to the left and you have a person wearing a Genie 3 T-shirt. It can just materialize things in the world, but that doesn't mean it just pops in front of you. Ideally, we want it to be integrated in and make sense in the world, because it's easy to just drop something that looks very artificial. We want it to actually be integrated, to look real. The model eventually wants to make things that look like the training data, which ultimately should be realistic. So somehow, additional conditioning information that's integral to the next-frame generation process, as opposed to we're just going to drop this thing in the middle of the view.

items.question: How do you understand the limitations of Genie 3’s action space for agents?
items.object: Genie 3’s agent action space
items.answer:
Currently the action space is relatively constrained. We can have the agent navigate. We have some actions like jumping or opening doors, but it's relatively basic in terms of the semantics of the action that the agent is taking. Promptable world events give us control over the world, but they're not necessarily agent-centric actions. This is definitely something that we hope to improve and expand in the future.

It's quite challenging, but for anything agent-like, if we want the agent to take more complex actions, not just walk around but actually be able to pick up things, maybe do typing of some code, or talk to a different agent, there are many things that can happen in the world. It's quite a challenging problem because we operate in the world as people in a very physical way. We use our hands, our feet to walk; we have an embodied presence. When we take away all of these and are left with visuals, with pixels only, it's much harder to define what actions should actually happen. When you open the door, you go and grab the knob and move it, and pull it towards you. There's a sequence of micro-actions taking place. I think this is a challenging question of how to model this space of actions. It's definitely a limitation and an opportunity to expand the capabilities.

items.question: What excites you about being able to step into a generated world anchored in a real-world location?
items.object: Interactive generated worlds anchored in real-world locations
items.answer: To me, the ability to step into a world that you created or someone else created, but then you can actually perceive it, see it, interact with it, is huge, which can be applied to so many things, from entertainment, which is very obvious—interactive street view, for example. It can be somewhat anchored in the real world but take it somewhere else. It reminds me of a startup I worked for a long time ago, and we had a game placed in downtown San Francisco. items.question: Why do you see personalized generated environments as potentially powerful for helping people accomplish things they wouldn't expect of themselves?
items.object: Personalized generated environments for seeing oneself accomplish unexpected things
items.answer: I think there are other really interesting applications for people, maybe not necessarily entertainment. It can be education, for example. It can be helping people see themselves accomplishing something they wouldn't have expected themselves to. There is something very strong about seeing yourself maybe accomplishing something, and then it kind of makes you—it's a bit of a psychological perspective, but I think it's very powerful. The personalization aspect of being able to go into the environment, walk around, maybe prompt it in a way that looks very similar to your house, for example. items.question: How do you think about discovering potential applications for Genie 3 at this early stage?
items.object: Exploring applications of Genie 3
items.answer: My point is that we don't necessarily know where this technology will go, and it's very early days for that. That's why we had some trusted testers or academics interact with the model initially. We wanted to get some feedback, and we hope over time to learn more about the capabilities and the applications that people are excited about.
